frase_gancho.texto: A clay dancer with music in her legs.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the festival, we move on to the landscape that surrounded it. Look for the duck-shaped vessel, which takes us back to the lake where these people lived.

guion_corto.texto: This small clay figure from Tlatilco, about ten to fourteen centimeters tall, is a dancer. She stands with her torso bare, her arms slightly outstretched, and a conical headdress on her head. The most curious detail is in her legs: she wears bands covered in small spheres, which look like bells or strings of dried seeds. It is a memory of sound: with every step, the dancer’s body rang out, and the whole village danced in time. In these farming communities, music and dance accompanied the planting and the harvest. This figure is not merely decoration: it lets us glimpse a celebration from more than three thousand years ago.

guion_largo.texto:
Almost everything archaeology knows about the music of three thousand years ago is silence. Flutes break, voices vanish, and footsteps are erased. That is why this figurine is so valuable: it does not preserve the sound, but it left it drawn on the legs of a dancer.

Look at her attire. Her torso is bare and her arms are slightly open, like someone following a rhythm. On her head she wears a cone-shaped cap. And from her ankles to her calves, a covering of small clay beads that imitate bells or strings of dried seeds. Bands with seeds or bells were tied to the legs to mark the step: with every footfall, they rang.

This custom is so resilient that it still exists. The Yaqui dancers of the Northwest, whom you will find in the Northwest Hall, tie strings of cocoons filled with small pebbles around their legs, which they call tenábaris. And in some dances of Mexica tradition, strings of seeds called ayoyotes are used. In other words: what this clay woman wore three thousand years ago is still worn by dancers today.

Why did people dance? For agricultural peoples, dance was a way of asking. With the body they called for rain, gave thanks for the harvest, and accompanied the dead. The sound of the bells, moreover, resembled the sound of rain falling on the cornfield and the buzzing of insects. To dance was to cast a spell with the feet on the packed earth of the plaza.

There is another reason why dance mattered so much. These communities had no writing, and their memory lived in what was done with the body: songs, stories, processions, and dances that were repeated year after year. To dance was to preserve the history of the people. That is why dancers appear in tombs and in figures: they were a portrait of what the village considered important.

Think of it alongside the other pieces in this display case. [The Acrobat](mna_s03_acrobata_tlatilco) twisting, the little face split in two, the women with elaborate hairstyles: everything speaks of a village that thought of itself through the body, through paint, through rhythm. Here you see the happiest moment of that life: the festival.

One more detail about her clothing: she wears little, and everything she wears makes a sound or moves. The conical headdress, the open arms, the legs covered in small spheres: every element is designed so that the movement can be seen and heard. Whoever modeled her knew what a dance is, and wanted it to show.

And notice a detail that says a great deal. This village, which buried its dead beneath the floors of its houses, also made figures to celebrate life. Those who learned to live alongside death surely had every reason to dance. And if you look at what comes next, this clay dancer is a great-great-grandmother of the [Viejitos (Little Old Men)](mna_s14_mascara_viejitos) of Michoacán, of the Voladores (Flyers) of Papantla, and of the Yaqui dancers, whom you will meet upstairs.

texto: Look for the bands of little spheres on the ankles and calves: they look like bells or seeds
Notice the conical headdress on her head
Observe the posture of her arms: she seems to be following a rhythm

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Tlatilco figurines were simply toys for children.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were found in houses and tombs, and many appear to be linked to rituals, festivals, and beliefs about fertility; they were not merely toys.
